title: Cyclobenzaprine and Alcohol: Risks, Timing, and Warning Signs
excerpt: Can you drink on cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril)? Why the muscle relaxant and alcohol stack sedation, how long to wait after your last dose, and the warning signs that need help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril)? Why it and alcohol stack sedation, how long to wait after your last dose, and warning signs that need help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** cyclobenzaprine (brand names Flexeril, Amrix, and Fexmid) and alcohol should not be mixed. Both slow down your brain and nervous system, and together they add up to more drowsiness, dizziness, poor coordination, and slowed reactions than either one alone. The prescribing label says plainly that cyclobenzaprine "may enhance the effects of alcohol, barbiturates, and other CNS depressants." Even a single drink can leave you far more impaired than you expect, which is how falls, car crashes, and dangerous mix-ups with other sedating drugs happen. This guide explains why the two clash, how long to wait after your last dose, what makes the combination more dangerous, and the warning signs that mean you should get help.

**The quick rules:** The safest plan is not to drink while you're taking cyclobenzaprine. Most courses last only two to three weeks, so skipping alcohol is usually a short-term ask. If you've already had a drink, don't take another dose on top of it to "help you sleep," don't drive, and don't add other sleepy medicines like Benadryl, sleep aids, opioids, or benzodiazepines. If you take cyclobenzaprine with an antidepressant or tramadol, talk to your doctor before drinking at all. If someone is very hard to wake, confused, has a racing or irregular heartbeat, or is breathing slowly, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and the exact medicines you take. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking** if you've been prescribed cyclobenzaprine, especially if you also take antidepressants, opioids, tramadol, anxiety or sleep medicines, or gabapentin, or if you're over 65 or have heart, liver, or thyroid problems. **Call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US)** if someone who mixed cyclobenzaprine and alcohol is hard to wake, confused, seeing things that aren't there, has a pounding or irregular heartbeat, has a seizure, or is breathing slowly or shallowly.

## What Cyclobenzaprine Is and How It Works

Cyclobenzaprine is a prescription muscle relaxant. Doctors use it for short-term relief of muscle spasms from strains, sprains, and acute back or neck injuries, usually alongside rest and physical therapy. It's one of the most commonly prescribed muscle relaxants in the United States.

You'll see it under a few names:

- **Flexeril** was the original brand. The brand has been discontinued in the US, but many people (and many doctors) still call the drug "Flexeril."
- **Generic cyclobenzaprine** tablets, usually 5 mg or 10 mg, typically taken up to three times a day.
- **Amrix** is an extended-release capsule (15 mg or 30 mg) taken once a day.
- **Fexmid** is another brand of the 7.5 mg tablet.

Here's the part most people don't know: cyclobenzaprine doesn't work directly on your muscles. It acts in the brainstem and central nervous system, and it is chemically very close to the older tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline. That family resemblance explains most of its side effects. Like tricyclics, cyclobenzaprine:

- **Blocks histamine**, the same action that makes Benadryl sleepy. This is a big part of why cyclobenzaprine causes so much drowsiness.
- **Blocks acetylcholine** (an "anticholinergic" effect), which causes dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, trouble urinating, and, in some people, confusion.
- **Affects serotonin signaling**, which is why it carries a warning about serotonin syndrome when combined with certain antidepressants and other drugs.
- **Can affect heart rhythm**, especially at high doses. That's why the label says not to use it after a recent heart attack or in people with certain heart rhythm problems, heart failure, or an overactive thyroid.

Drowsiness is the most common side effect even without alcohol. In the clinical trials behind the label, it was reported by roughly a third of people taking standard doses, along with dry mouth and dizziness. In other words, the drug is already sedating on its own before you add anything to it.

## Why Cyclobenzaprine and Alcohol Don't Mix

Alcohol is also a central nervous system depressant. It slows reaction time, dulls judgment, and makes you sleepy. When you combine it with cyclobenzaprine, you're stacking two sedating effects on the same system. The result isn't simple addition; for many people the combination feels much stronger than they'd predict from either one alone.

### More sedation and impairment

The main, everyday risk is heavy drowsiness and impairment. People describe feeling "knocked out," dizzy, unsteady on their feet, and foggy. Practically, that means:

- **Falls and injuries.** Ironically, many people take cyclobenzaprine because they've hurt their back. A fall while unsteady can make an injury worse. The risk is higher for older adults.
- **Unsafe driving.** The label already warns that cyclobenzaprine can impair your ability to drive or operate machinery. Alcohol on top of it makes that much worse, even at amounts that would normally feel mild.
- **Poor judgment about dosing.** People who are drowsy and a bit drunk are more likely to forget they've already taken a dose, or to take extra to try to sleep.

### Breathing and the "other sedatives" problem

On its own, cyclobenzaprine is not known for dangerously slowing breathing the way opioids and benzodiazepines can. The bigger breathing risk comes when cyclobenzaprine and alcohol are combined with a third sedating drug, such as an opioid painkiller, a benzodiazepine like Xanax or Valium, gabapentin, or a sleep aid. Each one adds more depression of the brain's drive to breathe. That stacking is where overdoses and deaths involving muscle relaxants usually show up.

This matters because people with back injuries are often given more than one of these drugs at the same time, sometimes by different doctors. If you've got a muscle relaxant and a painkiller in your cabinet, alcohol becomes a much bigger deal.

### Anticholinergic effects and confusion

Both alcohol and cyclobenzaprine's anticholinergic action can cloud thinking. Together they can cause confusion, disorientation, and, at higher doses, agitation or hallucinations. Older adults are especially sensitive to this. It's one reason the American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, a widely used list of medicines to be cautious with in people over 65, advises generally avoiding muscle relaxants like cyclobenzaprine in older adults.

### Heart rhythm

Because cyclobenzaprine is related to tricyclic antidepressants, high doses can cause a fast heartbeat and, in overdose, dangerous heart rhythm problems. Heavy drinking can also trigger irregular heart rhythms in some people. For a normal dose and a single drink, this isn't the main concern, but it's one more reason not to take extra cyclobenzaprine or drink heavily while on it, and to take a racing or irregular heartbeat seriously.

## Flexeril and Alcohol: Is It Any Different?

No. Flexeril is simply the original brand name for cyclobenzaprine, so everything on this page applies to Flexeril, generic cyclobenzaprine, Fexmid, and Amrix alike. The active drug and its interaction with alcohol are the same.

The one practical difference is with **Amrix**, the extended-release version. It releases the drug slowly over the day, so levels stay up longer after each dose, and its half-life is longer than the standard tablets. That means the "wait before drinking" window is generally longer with Amrix, not shorter.

## Can You Have One Drink on Cyclobenzaprine?

The label doesn't set a "safe" number of drinks. It simply warns that the drug can make alcohol's effects stronger. That's why the standard advice from pharmacists and doctors is to avoid alcohol while you're taking it.

In real life, here's how to think about it:

- **Even one drink** will probably hit you harder than usual. There is no amount the label calls safe, so whether any alcohol is okay for you is a question only your prescriber or pharmacist can answer. If you do drink, don't drive or do anything that needs coordination.
- **Several drinks** raise the risk of heavy sedation, falls, vomiting while very drowsy, and poor decisions about medication.
- **Any drinking plus another sedating medicine** (opioid, benzodiazepine, gabapentin, sleep aid, or sedating antihistamine) is a different situation. Don't do it without talking to your doctor first.
- **Any drinking if you're over 65, have heart, liver, or thyroid problems, or take an antidepressant** is also a "talk to your doctor first" situation.

If your doctor has said an occasional drink is fine for you, take that seriously as advice about *your* situation. If you haven't asked, ask. It's a normal question and pharmacists field it all the time.

## How Long After Cyclobenzaprine Can You Drink?

This is the most common question, and the answer is longer than most people expect.

Cyclobenzaprine stays in the body a long time. The label lists an average elimination half-life of about 18 hours for the standard tablets, with a wide range from person to person (roughly 8 to 37 hours). The half-life is the time it takes your body to clear half of the drug. A common rule of thumb is that it takes around five half-lives for a drug to be mostly gone, which for an average person on standard tablets works out to roughly three to four days. Amrix, the extended-release capsule, has a longer half-life still, around a day and a half on average.

Half-life is longer in older adults and in people with liver problems, so the drug lingers even more for them.

What that means in practice:

- **While you're taking it on a regular schedule,** there's always meaningful drug in your system. There's no "safe gap" between doses to drink in.
- **After a single dose,** the strongest effect is in the first several hours, but the drug is still active the next day. Many people notice next-day grogginess even without alcohol.
- **After you stop,** waiting at least a few days before drinking gives your body time to clear most of it. Longer is safer if you're older, have liver problems, or took Amrix.

There's no exact cutoff that applies to everyone. If you want a number for your situation, ask your pharmacist. They can look at your dose, how long you took it, and your other medicines.

## How Long After Drinking Can You Take Cyclobenzaprine?

The reverse question matters too. If you've been drinking and your back is killing you, it's tempting to take your muscle relaxant before bed. That's exactly when the combination is most likely to hit hard, because both drugs peak around the same time while you're falling asleep.

A sensible approach is to wait until the alcohol is out of your system before taking a dose. The body clears roughly one standard drink per hour on average, though this varies a lot with body size, food, and genetics. After a heavier night, that can mean waiting until the next morning or later. Our guide on [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explains the timing in more detail.

If you're unsure, skip the dose. Missing one dose of a muscle relaxant is rarely a big problem. Doubling up on sedation is.

## Cyclobenzaprine, Alcohol, and the Next-Day Hangover

Even if nothing dangerous happens, mixing the two tends to make the next morning worse:

- **Grogginess and "fog."** Cyclobenzaprine's long half-life already causes next-morning drowsiness for many people. Alcohol's disrupted sleep adds to it.
- **Dry mouth and thirst.** The drug's anticholinergic effect dries you out, and alcohol makes you lose fluid. Together you can feel unusually parched.
- **Dizziness.** Both cause it, and the effect can linger.
- **Constipation and nausea.** Cyclobenzaprine slows the gut, and alcohol irritates the stomach.

### What not to do the morning after

- **Don't take a sleep aid or Benadryl** to "sleep it off." Diphenhydramine is both sedating and anticholinergic, the same two effects you're already getting from cyclobenzaprine. Our [Benadryl for hangovers](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) guide covers why it's a poor choice even without a muscle relaxant on board.
- **Don't take extra cyclobenzaprine** because your back hurts after a night out. Stick to your prescribed schedule, and consider skipping a dose if you're still feeling the alcohol.
- **Be thoughtful about pain relievers.** Acetaminophen and ibuprofen don't add sedation, but each has its own issues with alcohol. Read our guides on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) and [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) before reaching for either.
- **Don't drive** until you feel completely clear, and give it extra time beyond that.

What does help is the boring stuff: water, a light meal, and rest.

## What Else Makes the Combination More Dangerous

The biggest risks come from what *else* is in the mix. Check your medicine cabinet and tell your doctor and pharmacist about everything you take, including over-the-counter products.

### Opioid painkillers

Hydrocodone, oxycodone, codeine, and tramadol are often prescribed alongside cyclobenzaprine for back injuries. Opioids slow breathing, and adding a muscle relaxant and alcohol stacks the sedation further. This is the combination to take most seriously.

### Benzodiazepines and sleep medicines

Drugs like alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium), lorazepam (Ativan), and sleep aids like zolpidem (Ambien) all add sedation. See our guide on [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) for why that pairing is already risky without a muscle relaxant.

### Gabapentin and pregabalin

These are often prescribed for nerve pain from back injuries. The FDA has warned about serious breathing problems when gabapentinoids are combined with other central nervous system depressants. Our [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) guide covers this in detail.

### Antidepressants and tramadol: serotonin syndrome

Cyclobenzaprine carries a warning about serotonin syndrome when combined with SSRIs (like sertraline or fluoxetine), SNRIs (like duloxetine or venlafaxine), tricyclic antidepressants, tramadol, bupropion, meperidine, and some other drugs. It must not be taken with MAO inhibitors or within 14 days of stopping one. Serotonin syndrome can cause agitation, sweating, fever, fast heartbeat, muscle twitching or stiffness, and diarrhea. Alcohol doesn't cause serotonin syndrome, but it can mask early signs and makes the overall picture harder to read. If you take any of these, ask your doctor before drinking.

### Sedating antihistamines and "PM" products

Diphenhydramine (Benadryl, and the "PM" in many night-time pain relievers), doxylamine (Unisom and NyQuil), and similar antihistamines add both sedation and anticholinergic effects. They're easy to take without thinking of them as "drugs," which is exactly why they're a common hidden risk.

### Cannabis

Cannabis also causes drowsiness and slower reactions. Combining it with cyclobenzaprine and alcohol adds a third layer of impairment.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

- **Adults over 65.** They clear cyclobenzaprine more slowly, are more prone to confusion and falls, and are generally advised to avoid muscle relaxants like this one.
- **People with liver problems,** including those who drink heavily on a regular basis. The liver breaks down cyclobenzaprine, so impaired liver function means higher, longer-lasting levels. The label advises caution and lower doses in mild liver impairment and does not recommend it in moderate or severe impairment.
- **People with heart conditions** such as arrhythmias, heart block, heart failure, or a recent heart attack, and people with an overactive thyroid. Cyclobenzaprine is not recommended for them at all.
- **People with glaucoma or trouble urinating,** because the anticholinergic effects can worsen both.
- **Anyone taking more than one sedating medicine,** especially opioids, benzodiazepines, or gabapentin.
- **Anyone who has to drive, work at heights, or operate machinery,** even the day after.

## Is Cyclobenzaprine Misused With Alcohol?

Cyclobenzaprine is not a controlled substance in the US, and it isn't generally considered to have much potential for misuse on its own. But some people do combine it with alcohol on purpose to intensify the sedating effect. That's a risky thing to do because the effect is unpredictable, the drug lasts a long time, and it's easy to end up with far more on board than you intended. If you notice yourself reaching for a muscle relaxant to enhance drinking, that's worth a conversation with your doctor.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

Mild extra drowsiness after a drink is common. These signs are not, and they need medical help.

**Call 911 right away if someone who has taken cyclobenzaprine and alcohol:**

- Can't be woken up, or is very hard to wake
- Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly
- Has blue or gray lips or fingertips
- Has a seizure
- Has a very fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat, or chest pain
- Is very confused, agitated, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there
- Has collapsed or fainted

**While you wait for help:** stay with the person, keep them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and don't give them anything to eat or drink. Don't try to "walk it off" or let them sleep it off alone. If you can, collect their medicine bottles to show the paramedics.

**Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US)** if someone took more cyclobenzaprine than prescribed, or you're not sure whether a combination is safe, even if they seem fine for now. Poison Control is free, confidential, and staffed by experts around the clock.

**See a doctor soon** if you notice signs of serotonin syndrome (agitation, sweating, fever, muscle twitching or stiffness, fast heartbeat) while taking cyclobenzaprine with an antidepressant or tramadol, or if you keep feeling confused, dizzy, or unsteady while on the drug.

## Practical Tips if Your Doctor Says a Drink Is Okay

Some doctors will say an occasional drink is acceptable for a particular patient. If that's you:

1. **Stay within the exact limit your prescriber gave you,** and have it with food. If they didn't give you a number, ask before drinking.
2. **Don't drink close to a dose.** Space them as far apart as your schedule allows.
3. **Stay home.** No driving, cycling, or anything that needs balance or quick reactions.
4. **Skip other sedating products** that night, including sleep aids and "PM" pain relievers.
5. **Drink water** alongside, since cyclobenzaprine already dries you out.
6. **Let someone know** you've mixed them, especially if you live alone.
7. **Pay attention to how you feel.** If you feel much more affected than usual, stop drinking and don't take another dose until you're clear.

## What About DHM and Other Hangover Supplements?

Some people take hangover supplements when they drink. It's worth being clear about what they can and can't do here.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the brain's GABA receptors. Most of the research is in animals and lab studies, with limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the interaction between cyclobenzaprine and alcohol, and it does **not** make it safe to drink while taking a muscle relaxant. Because DHM's possible effects involve the same GABA system that many sedating drugs act on, it's sensible to check with your doctor or pharmacist before combining it with cyclobenzaprine or any other sedating medicine. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers this in more detail.

Once you've finished your course of cyclobenzaprine and are back to occasional social drinking, DHM is one option some people use. Popular choices include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

No supplement should change how you use a prescription medicine. Follow your prescription and your doctor's advice about alcohol, whatever else you take.

## The Bottom Line

- Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril, Amrix, Fexmid) and alcohol both slow your nervous system, and together they cause much more drowsiness, dizziness, and impairment than either alone.
- The safest plan is to avoid alcohol for the usually short time you're taking it.
- The drug lasts a long time in the body. Waiting a few days after your last dose before drinking is sensible, and longer if you're older, have liver problems, or took Amrix.
- The real danger multiplies when you add a third sedating drug, such as an opioid, a benzodiazepine, gabapentin, or a sleep aid.
- If you take an antidepressant or tramadol, ask your doctor before drinking because of the serotonin syndrome warning.
- If someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, confused, or has an irregular heartbeat, call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking cyclobenzaprine?**

It's best not to. Cyclobenzaprine and alcohol both slow down your brain and nervous system, and the prescribing label warns that cyclobenzaprine may enhance the effects of alcohol. Together they can cause heavy drowsiness, dizziness, poor coordination, and slowed reactions. Most courses last only two to three weeks, so the simplest plan is to skip alcohol until you've finished. If you want to drink, ask your doctor or pharmacist first.

**Is Flexeril and alcohol the same as cyclobenzaprine and alcohol?**

Yes. Flexeril is the original brand name for cyclobenzaprine. Generic cyclobenzaprine, Fexmid, and the extended-release Amrix all contain the same active drug, and all carry the same warning about alcohol. With Amrix, the drug stays in your system longer, so the wait before drinking is generally longer.

**How long after taking cyclobenzaprine can I drink alcohol?**

Longer than most people expect. The label lists an average half-life of about 18 hours for standard tablets, with a wide range between people, and it takes several half-lives for the drug to mostly clear. For an average person that works out to roughly three to four days after the last dose, and longer for older adults, people with liver problems, or anyone taking extended-release Amrix. Your pharmacist can give you a more specific answer for your dose.

**Can I have one beer on cyclobenzaprine?**

The label doesn't set a safe number of drinks; it advises against combining them. There's no amount the label calls safe, and even one drink will probably hit you much harder than usual, so don't drive. Whether any alcohol is okay for you is a question for your prescriber or pharmacist. If you're over 65, have heart, liver, or thyroid problems, or take an opioid, benzodiazepine, gabapentin, antidepressant, or tramadol, talk to your doctor before having any alcohol.

**Can I take cyclobenzaprine after drinking to help me sleep?**

It's not a good idea. Taking it at bedtime after drinking means both drugs peak while you're falling asleep, which is when the combined sedation hits hardest. Wait until the alcohol has cleared (roughly one standard drink per hour on average, though this varies), or skip that dose. Missing one dose of a muscle relaxant is rarely a problem.

**What happens if you mix cyclobenzaprine and alcohol?**

Most often, much stronger drowsiness, dizziness, unsteadiness, and slowed thinking than either causes alone, plus a worse next morning with grogginess and dry mouth. More serious effects, such as confusion, hallucinations, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or dangerously slowed breathing, are more likely with large amounts or when a third sedating drug like an opioid, benzodiazepine, or gabapentin is involved. Call 911 if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, or confused.

**Is it dangerous to take cyclobenzaprine with alcohol and an antidepressant?**

It can be. Cyclobenzaprine carries a warning about serotonin syndrome when combined with SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, tramadol, bupropion, and some other drugs, and it must not be used with MAO inhibitors. Alcohol adds sedation and can make early warning signs harder to spot. If you take any of these medicines, ask your doctor before drinking.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on cyclobenzaprine?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the interaction between cyclobenzaprine and alcohol, and it does not make the combination safe. Because DHM may act on the brain's GABA system, which many sedating drugs also affect, check with your doctor or pharmacist before combining it with cyclobenzaprine or any other sedating medicine.
